What other tense and voice use this iterative form? How is it made? H. 410 D.; C. 334; G. 119, 10. It is not confined to Homer, but is found among the epic writers, the Dorians, in Herodotus, and occasionally in the Attic poets. — biēphi . . . ēsan, "for in strength mightier were they." — biēphi; H. 206 D., 609. The Phaeacians are an ease-loving people and care not for the bow and the quiver; Odyssey 8.248, 6.270. Polyphemus stolidly answers Odysseus' appeal to the rights of guestship by declaring that he must be a simpleton or come from afar, if he thinks the Cyclopes regard either Zeus or any of the gods, epeiē poly pherteroí eimen, Odyssey 9.276. This epeiē exemplifies the de of the passage before us, where, as often, it expresses the reason and stands for epei or gar, not only in Homer, but also in later Greek, though less frequently: on Odyssey 6.169.

7. anastēsas, "having made them to rise up." What distinction between the transitive and intransitive tenses of histēmi? H. 416; C. 329. Migration under pressure from more powerful neighbors must have been a strong element among the causes that peopled Europe out of Asia. An historical parallel to the case of the Phaeacians is that of the Phocaeans of Ionia, who, being hard pressed by the Persians under Harpagus, launched their penteconters, embarked their wives and children, household effects and all, and sailed away to Corsica.

8. eisen de Scheriē, "and seated them in Scheria." The omission of the preposition is poetic; H. 612. Even in Homer, where this is most common, it is a comparatively rare construction, and still more so in the lyric and tragic writers. Some read d' en here. The Phaeacians, with their marvellous ships and devotion to the sea, would, like the Phocaeans, think only of removal by sea in order to free themselves from such troublesome neighbors. But

BOOK VI. 51

to be rid of all troublesome neighbors, that they might lead in security their life of unruffled ease, they would be likely to choose an island home. See on ζ 204, η 9, 239. Was Scheria a mere figment of the poet's imagination without a local habitation, or was it the geographical Corcyra, as was popularly believed by the Greeks at least as early as the days of Thucydides? — ἀλφηστάων, not found in the Iliad, and but twice elsewhere in the Odyssey; if derived from ἄλφι, ἔδειν, it is equivalent to "eating grain"; cf. θ 222. But the older interpretation from ἀλφεῖν, to acquire, is "gain-seeking," and the phrase (for it is habitually used with ἄνδρες) is distinctly applied to merchants in the Hymn to Apollo, and in Aeschylus. Thus it has an added significance here, for the Phaeacians are not only remote from all other men, but not even merchants visit them; cf. ζ 205, 278, η 9, θ 161–64.

9. ἀμφὶ . . . πόλει, "and around, a wall he ran for a city." — ἀμφὶ is adverbial; see on ν 119. ἀμφί with the dative has in Homer, like most prepositions, a strong tendency to stand at the beginning of the clause, especially with δέ. While its position is thus fixed, its noun is more or less free to subserve the poet's convenience in the metrical and rhetorical construction of his line; cf. ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρα φίλην βάλεν ἔγχεῖ, φ 433; ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρας δειρῇ βάλλ' Ὀδυσῇι, ψ 207; ἀμφὶ δὲ παιδὶ φίλῳ βάλε πήχεε, ρ 38: also η 142, θ 426, 434. The compound ἀμφελαύνω never came into use. — ἔλασσε: in the figure employed the wall is regarded as a creature to be driven: ζ 82, η 86, 113, 109; on η 29. — πόλει; H. 597, ν 73. — ἐδείματο: why is the final vowel not elided? H. 67 D. a; G. 1, 2; C. 63 D. We may not suppose by the arrangement of this line that the people were left shelterless till the wall was built. It is an example of the common Homeric figure of "the later before the earlier," or putting-the-cart-before-the-horse. In a series of objects closely connected, our poet is fond of naming that first which strikes the eye first or most prominently, in viewing them as a whole: θ 455.

10. νηοὺς. It has been concluded by some from this passage that no Homeric city was without its temples; few, however, are actually mentioned. We have that of Athene at Athens, η 81, and Troy, Z 88; that of Apollo at Pytho, θ 80, Troy, and Chryse. One of Poseidon is implied ζ 266, in Scheria, and another at

52 NOTES.

Helice, Book VIII line 203; cf. Book XVI line 185, Book IV line 347, Book III line 274. Otherwise, the Greeks worshipped at altars and in groves; cf. Book VI lines 162, 291.

11. ἤδη, "already," before the period of our story. — κηρί. Of the various words used by Homer to signify doom or fate, κήρ is nearest to a distinct personification, and is of the darkest color, always implying death. It is also the fate of the individual, not of humanity. Compare Book VII line 197. — "Αἰδόσδε," "Hadesward." In the brevity of a familiar phrase the local particle δε has been appended to the genitive, where it belongs to an accusative that is understood. The fuller form of expression, as found elsewhere in the poems, is "into Hades," "into the house of Hades," "into the halls of Hades." The Aïdes of Homer is always a person, the youngest brother of Zeus, who obtained in the allotment of sovereignty the rule of the world of the dead. The entrance to his "House" is beside the Ocean-Stream, where it empties into the central sea. Hard by the Cimmerians dwell, and the whole region is wrapped forever in cloud and darkness. Odysseus sails thither from Circe's isle, and the shades are sent up for his inspection. The condition of the dead, though without punishment except for great offenders like Tantalus, is pitiable. "Seek not to comfort me in death," exclaims the shade of Achilles; "rather had I the lot of the wretchedest laborer upon earth than be king over all the dead;" Book XI line 488.

12. τότ', at the time of the story, as opposed to that of Nausithous and of the poet; cf. νῦν, Book VII line 68. — θεῶν . . . εἰδώς, "with wisdom from the gods endowed;" on Book VIII line 584. This god-given wisdom is not a favor shown to Alcinous alone; all conspicuous external and internal characteristics, in general, are received directly from on high; Book VIII lines 167, 488, 457, Book VI lines 18, 229. The Homeric man had ever before him the immediate interposition and guiding hand of Providence; on Book VI line 172. — ἄπο; Hadley's Grammar section 102 D. Anastrophe of this preposition occurs also at Book VI line 18, Book VII line 152, Book VIII lines 88, 411, 457; on Book VI line 15.

13. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις 'Αθήνη, "the goddess, luminous-eyed Athene." — γλαυκῶπις belongs to 'Αθήνη, not to θεά, as shown by its frequent occurrence with 'Αθήνη alone, but never with θεά alone. Our poetic translators usually treat this as an epithet of color; but it is more than probable that the idea of color does not enter into it at all. γλαυκός occurs once of the flashing sea, and γλαυκιόων

BOOK VI. 53

describes the eye of a lion, when, reaching the height of his wrath, he makes his rush at the hunters. This is the key to its force in glaukopis, representing the brightening flash of the eye under the influence of feeling. Athene is the goddess of war and the goddess of wisdom. In the one capacity the eye is kindled by martial fury; in the other by the power of mighty conceptions. The poet has developed a phase of it, Iliad 200: "and his eyes shone terribly." Schliemann's "owl-faced" is unproved.

14. "To Odysseus" (dative form): what is this in Attic? Hadley 189 D. The final syllable is lengthened by the probable doubling of the initial liquid of the following word in pronunciation; Hadley 87 D. This in thesis is rare; Iliad E 358. The word megas ("great") and its derivatives quite constantly lengthen a preceding short vowel; Odyssey Book 6, lines 62, 304; Book 7, lines 150, 180; Book 8, lines 9, 42, 227, 434, 520; Book 13, lines 2, 8, 13, 51, 121; cf. Book 7, line 145. — metioosa ("devising"), how is it formed? Hadley 370 D.; Goodwin 120; Curtius 243; on Book 8, line 574.

15. imen ("let us go"), Book 6, line 50. — thalamon ("chamber") is best placed in the second story of the palace; Iliad B 514, Iliad Pi 184. — polydaidalon, "richly wrought;" compare the description of the palace, Book 7, lines 83-97. — eni, Book 8, line 220; Book 11, line 367; on Book 6, lines 12, 262.

16. koimat', "was sleeping." — phuen ("figure"); Hadley 549; on Book 6, line 152.

17. Nausicaa is here introduced for the first time, and the poet has emphasized the fact by placing the name as the first word in the line. — megaletoros ("great-hearted") is Virgil's magnanimus, and is used by Homer not only of Aeneas several times, but of a number of other warriors, both Greeks and Trojans, most constantly of Odysseus. It is also applied to the Trojans as a people, the Paphlagonians, the Phlegyans, Myrmidons, and Eteocretans. It commonly has a good sense, "great-souled." Here it pictures that large-heartedness which Alcinous displays in his hospitality towards Odysseus.

18. par, "near by;" supply koimonto ("they were sleeping"). — The word amphipolos is always feminine, as therapon is masculine; and the former is a slave, while the latter is a freeman. Noble ladies are regularly attended by two amphipoloi, and are always accompanied by them when appearing in public. Here they sleep in the maiden's chamber, one on each side of the door, to guard the entrance. — The Graces of Homer, like his Hours, Fates, and Cyclopes, have no definite number, but are more than three. He conceives them mainly as

54 NOTES.

the attendants and handmaids of Aphrodite, and as such they doubtless came with her worship from Babylonia through Cyprus. Hence their earlier number would be two, as we see them in the Babylonian Isdubar Epic, and some of the Cypriote groups, and as they were worshipped in Lacedaemon and at Athens (Pausanias IX. 35). Elsewhere in Homer it is the gods that bestow beauty, Athene, Hera, and Aphrodite being especially mentioned as possessing that power. Here the beauty conferred by the handmaids of Aphrodite upon the handmaids of Nausicaa is remarkable, but it is inferior to that of the princess (Book VI, lines 108–9), which is the gift of the gods; Book VIII, line 457.

19. "stahmoin," Book VI line 82, Book VIII line 458.—Observe that "hekas" and its derivatives usually have the digamma; Book VI line 8; but not so in Book VII lines 91 and 321.— "epekeinto," "rested thereon," that is, upon the door-posts, which would occur only when closed; for the doors consisted of two valves turning, not upon hinges, like ours, but each upon a pivot running into the lintel above and the threshold below. — "phaeinai"; see Book VII line 84.

20. "But she like a breath of wind sped to the couch of the maiden."— The particle "de" is fully adversative, meaning "but," though the doors were closed. The goddess passes in through the key-hole, along the strap of the key, like the phantom which she sends to comfort Penelope in her dreams, Book IV line 802, when Penelope is suffering a mother's agony at the intelligence that the suitors are plotting the death of Telemachus on his return from Sparta. — "epessunto": what other verb doubles sigma after augment? Hadley's Grammar, section 308 D.

21. "ste ... kephales," the regular formula for assuming a position when addressing a person so reclined; most commonly of dreams, as that of Agamemnon in Book II line 20; but not exclusively. Athene so appears to Odysseus, as he is rolling and tossing on his bed of skins, Book XX line 32; and Eurycleia takes this position when she hastens to awake Penelope and announce the presence of Odysseus after the destruction of the suitors, Book XXIII line 4. Hence it does not mean "hovering in air," as Hayman explains, but standing near the head and bending over it. Virgil applies the expression to Iris as she descends to release the soul of Dido: "She flies down and hovers above the head," Aeneid IV line 702.— "pros" must be taken by tmesis with "eeipen," and the construction of the two accusatives is after the analogy of "prosaoudao," and even "audao." Yet the real compound "proseipon" is

BOOK VI. 55

construed with the accusative of the person only, and the thing, if expressed, becomes the dative. Still, Aristophanes has "I will address a word to you" (προσείπω σ' ἔπος), Pax 520; cf. 522.

23. "they" (οἵ), Nausicaa. — ὁμηλικίη, "a parity of years;" the abstract used for the concrete, ὁμηλικίη in place of ὁμῆλιξ. This usage gives vigor and beauty to the sentence. It is naturally a poetic mode of expression, and therefore is more common in Greek than other languages, as this language grew up under the auspices of poetry (Jelf, G. G.). — κεχάριστο, "was dear," used as an imperfect; H. 712 a; G. 200, 6. A passive sense for deponent verbs, though rare in the present and imperfect, is more common in the other tenses.

24. μιν, in this formula, is governed by προσέφη ("addressed"), not by ἔεισαμ., as is proved by λ 241, where μιν disappears along with προσέφη.

25. Ναυσικάα: why not Ναυσικάη? H. 125 D. — τί νύ, "why, pray?" H. 552 a; G. 160, 2. — ὧδε μεθήμονα, "so remiss." — γείνατο; H. 416, 8. This mode of expression is more forcible than the simple "Why art thou?" since it represents the remissness in the light of an inborn characteristic, and thereby incites the maiden to greater zeal; so N 777, Δ 400, E 800, α 223. Am.

26. τοι, "to thy discredit," the ethical dative, repeated in μοι, 59. — ἀκηδέα is predicate; σιγαλόεντα is attributive to εἵματα ("garments"). σιγαλ. is an example of the standing or fixed epithet, the application of which becomes at times incongruous, because the speaker has in mind the normal and proper state of the object, rather than its condition at the time; cf. 74, θ 41, 378, λ 327, Φ 218. For the expression, as applied to garments, we may compare "gleaming like a star" (ἀστὴρ δ' ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν), ο 108, of the peplus presented by Helen to Telemachus as a memorial of her handiwork. "The king gave his six sons the finest clothes you ever set eyes on, so fine that the light gleamed from them a long way off." Dasent's Tales from the Norse.

27. γάμος, the marriage ceremonies, which appear to have consisted of a wedding feast, celebrated with profuse bounty (λ 414) for the relatives and friends by the father of the bride (α 277, δ 3). The song and the dance accompany the feast (ψ 135). No vow appears to have been taken, and the validity of the marriage consisted in the public avowal in these ceremonies; ζ 288. As evening drew on, the bride was conducted by the groom and

56 NOTES.

his relatives to the house of his father, where young sons customarily lived, and the procession is thus described as wrought by Hephaistos upon the shield of Achilles, two weddings having occurred on the same day:

"And in it he fashioned two fine cities of mortal men. In one there were marriages and feasts, and brides were being led from their chambers through the city beneath blazing torches, and the loud wedding-song arose; young men were whirling in the dance, and among them flutes and lyres sounded; and women stood admiring at each doorway." Iliad 18.490–96.

"And two fair populous towns were sculptured there;
In one were marriage pomp and revelry,
And brides in gay procession through the streets
'Neath blazing torches from their chambers borne,
While frequent rose the hymeneal song.
Youths whirled around in joyous dance, with sound
Of flute and harp; and, standing at their doors,
Admiring women on the pageant gazed." Derby.

ἵνα means "at which," referring to the γάμος [wedding]. — καλά, supply εἵματα [garments]. — αὐτήν, standing for σὲ αὐτήν, as the subject of ἔννυσθαι; this verb, used in the middle voice, retains only the accusative of the thing, while the person is implied by the voice itself.

28. τὰ δέ means "and others," as if τὰ μέν had preceded. A scholiast tells us that it was customary for brides to furnish garments to the friends of the groom. If so, this practice appears nowhere else alluded to. The reference here might be to the dowry, more precisely specified below at line 38; for it seems pointless to deny that some dowry went with the bride, in light of passages at α 277, β 132, δ 736, Ι 148, η 314, Hymn to Aphrodite 140; but see the note on ζ 159. Yet, provision for men's garments to clothe Odysseus seems necessary here, since the device at lines 60–5 is simply intended to develop the character of the princess; and, further, to suppose the bridal procession dressed in garments of the bride's providing gives greater point to the next two lines. — ἄγωνται: see H. 757; G. 232, 3; G. M. 61, 3; C. 554; cf. ζ 159, 262, 297, 303, θ 445, 511, 549, ν 155.

29. ἐκ τούτων means "from these things," that is, from her own fair adornment and ample provision for the groom's friends. — τοι is the dative ethical, meaning "look you," or "you must know." As here, it not unfrequently

BOOK VI. 57

directs the attention of the listener earnestly to some proverbial or general statement; cf. θ 329, 351, ν 130. It corresponds often to our colloquial "you know." — anabaínei, "mounts high among men." — phátis is only less lightly personified than Óssa, B 93, ω 413, and is conceived as rising higher and higher as it advances; cf. "my fame reaches heaven," ι 20, τ 333–34, the description of Eris, Δ 442, and Virgil's Fama, Aeneid IV. 176. The construction of the accusative is unusual, but see ξ 286, Euripides, Hecuba 928, 119.

30. esthle receives a double emphasis by its position at the end of the clause and the beginning of the line. This is a favorite artifice with our poet; see ζ 132, 182, 233, 274, 283, 284, 301, etc.

31. iomen, subjunctive of exhortation, showing the original connecting vowel instead of the later mode sign; Hadley 347 D. For the mode, see ζ 126, η 190, θ 31, 34; for the vowel, ζ 33, 126, 219, 232, 259, 262, etc. — plyneousal; H. 373. This future has the true stem plun-; the present is lengthened by the insertion of iota; H. 328 d. — "at dawn," a frequent Homeric formula, which was handed down in its essence to later Greek, as in Herodotus III. 86, Xenophon, Anabasis II. 3, 1; I. 7, 2. The dative is not used absolutely, as Jelf would have it, but is governed by hama. Homer regularly employs the present participle when speaking of the sun rising, but the aorist of its setting, as A 592; because we can follow the further course of the sun after it has risen, but no mortal eye sees it after it has set. (Classen, Beobachtungen, p. 59.)

32. "I will follow along." The simple dative of accompaniment with hepomai is often more clearly defined in Homer by hama, syn, meta. In like manner other verbs of following. hopedeō has hama in Homer, meta in Hesiod; homarteo, hama in Homer, syn in Sophocles. The Attic akoloutheo takes syn, and meta with the genitive. This tendency is further seen in compounds, such as synepomai, synephepomai, symparepomoi, synepakolutheō, symparakolutheō.

33. The first word of this line and the last are scanned with synizesis. — entyneai is aorist subjunctive. Why may it not contain a dactyl? H. 345, 2. — eti has long ultima; why? H. 87 D.; C. 77 D.

35. Connect "of all the Phaeacians" with "the best men"; cf. ζ 283, θ 36, 390. — hothi . . . autei, "where for thine ownself, too, is thy parentage;" hothi refers to dēmon. — autei is to be connected with toi, and the phrase is strengthened by kai; see 39. hothi has been referred to
3*

58 NOTES.

"aristees" as well as "demon." But, whichever is preferred, it has appeared weak and pointless to tell Nausicaa that she is a Phaeacian, or that she is noble. This has led Bekker and some others to omit the line. But they have not seen that the purpose of the poet here is to hint the fact that the princess is wooed by native suitors, and those only, and thus to intimate at this early stage how distasteful they are to her, and the effect which the coming of Odysseus may produce. For, as Mr. Gladstone has shown (Hom. Studies, III. p. 69), the distinction in Greece between the aristocracy and the royal family was so broad a one that the latter were accustomed to contract a marriage only with royalty beyond their own borders, as is the custom among the reigning families of Europe at the present day. Since Phaeacian life and manners are essentially Greek, simply a trifle more god-favored and effeminate, the same custom may be supposed to obtain in Scheria; and though all communication with the outer world is severed by their remoteness, yet there remains a lingering hope in the family that for the only daughter, the darling of them all, some Nausithous (Book η 56–62) may be thrown in their way by Providence, and she may thus be rescued from the nobles she despises (Book ζ 283), and sustain the dignity of her station. This will explain her secret wish that Odysseus will remain among them (Book ζ 245), the immediate supposition on the part of the gossiping populace (spoken, however, by Nausicaa herself, and so colored by her thought) that a stranger seen with her will become her husband (Book ζ 277), and the startling offer of his daughter's hand which Alcinous makes to a total stranger (Book η 313). Hence the line is not only not weak and pointless, but shows that the poet had in mind when it was composed the passages just cited, which have been the objects of strong suspicion. See further on those passages, and Proceedings of American Philological Association for 1879, p. 8.

36. "eothi pro," "in the morning early."—"pro," temporal adverb like "proi." This construction accords with the sequel, line 48, as also Book Λ 50, where the same phrase is used of a period later than the actual coming of Eos, Book Λ 1. "eothi" is then a temporal dative. If "pro" be made the post-positive preposition, "before" dawn, a double difficulty is assumed—the circumstances of the case, and the

BOOK VI. 59

The fact that θι is mainly a dative termination in its use, though ὅθι = οὗ, and αὐτόθι = αὐτοῦ.

37. ἅμαξαν: H. 65 D. — ἥ κεν ἄγῃσιν is a relative clause of purpose; cf. ζ 58, 114. How would this be expressed in prose, and how is it a sign of archaism? G. M. 65, 1, and Note 2, Rem.; G. 236. — ἄγῃσιν: In Attic, what active endings are dropped, and when? H. 361; G. 112, 2, Note.

38. ζώστρά occurs only here, but is equivalent to ζώνας, an important part of female attire, which here and in general must have been of some woven or knit material, to admit of washing. The only girdles for females whose material is specified by Homer are those of Circe and Calypso. They are of gold, but it is implied that they are of unusual splendor. That of Hera is adorned with a hundred tassels. — The πέπλος is the large uncut garment of the women, corresponding to the χλαῖνα or φᾶρος of the men, and worn like those over the more tightly fitting undergarment, the χιτών. They also served for other purposes, as offerings to the gods, coverings for thrones (η 96, etc.). — ῥήγεα, from the root ῥεγ, to dye, are colored rugs or thick woollen blankets, used commonly for the covering of the bedstead (η 336, ν 73, 118), though they are spread upon the thrones in Circe's palace. They would necessarily form a part of the dowry of a bride for the outfit of a new household, and all material fresh from the loom would need washing.

39. The conveyance is necessary for the vestments, "and in this way, too, for yourself (as the king's daughter) it is far more seemly than to go on foot." — καὶ δέ is an epic collocation; in Attic the words are habitually separated by the emphasized expression; ζ 60, 286, η 213; cf. η 327. — σοὶ αὐτῇ: Homer never compounds these pronouns, even when reflexive, but commonly places their components in juxtaposition, as ζ 60, θ 396. They are sometimes separated by light enclitics or conjunctions and the like (λ 369, 371, θ 211), or by one or more emphatic words (ζ 35, 39, 277). — κάλλιον: how does it differ from the Attic form? H. 222 D. — πόδεσσιν: note the various forms: θ 230, 253, 103.

40. ἀπὸ in the sense of "far from" is common in Homer, and regularly stands directly before its case, as ζ 220, λ 344; cf. ζ 294. Here it is best taken, perhaps, with the verb by tmesis, as ὃν οὐκέτι

60 NOTES.

"I declare that [he will be] away from his loved ones" (Odyssey σ 145). The subject is not uncommonly placed between the preposition and its verb; see η 283, θ 380, 475; on ζ 100. — πλυνοί, "laundry-pits;" on 86. — πόληος; Hadley's Grammar 186 D.; Curtius 157 D.

42. "Where they say the seat of the gods fast forever standeth." Many objections have been urged against the genuineness of lines 42–7. The description of Olympus has been declared inconsistent with that of the Iliad, so that the Chorizontes have found in it confirmation of their belief in the different authorship of the two poems. Mure reconciles this in the following way: "Olympus is here figured as a mountain, the sides and visible summit of which are for the most part enveloped in snow and clouds; while its extreme peak, where the palace of Jove was situated, free from all such atmospheric contamination, enjoyed a perpetual brilliancy and serenity. The confusion between heaven as a mountain and heaven as a sphere equally pervades both poems." Cf. Iliad Θ 19 and following, Τ 126 and following, Ο 18 and following, Odyssey υ 103–4, 113–14. So too, there are numerous inconsistencies in the Homeric picture of Hades and elsewhere, where the marvelous enters largely, as seen also in Virgil, and often in tales of wonder; see note on ζ 329. Again, φασί is said to be strange, applied as it is to a fact elsewhere so fully accepted by the poet; but cf. Ν 631, Ε 635, Ζ 100, Υ 105, 206, Β 783, Ω 615, μ 389–90; Virgil, Aeneid I. 731, III. 416, Conington on IV. 577; Horace, Odes III. 5, 41. It is the real world now and then peeping through the wonder-working element so constantly in sight. The passage has also been called irrelevant, because there is no reason why at this point we should be carried off to divine abodes. Episodes, however, are a striking feature of the Homeric style; and, as a detailed description of the dwelling-place of the gods is to be found nowhere else in the poems, it may be maintained that this splendid picture of the divine seat and the easy life there is but a fitting introduction to that of an earthly community which, in its local surroundings and luxurious living, approaches near to the gods. Set aside this passage altogether, and it might truly be said that the poet has painted a fairer Elysium for the god-connected man in the afterlife (δ 563–69), and a fairer Elysium for the Phaeacian upon earth, than he has anywhere given to his deities in heaven.

BOOK VI. 61

43. The word "ποτ'" connects to both the preceding and following clauses; compare ε 479, δ 566. Note that the subject of the verbs is "the seat of the gods" (θεῶν ἕδος), not Olympus as a whole. These lines are translated by Lucretius (On the Nature of Things, III. 18–22), when he is describing the rapt vision of the student of nature as he gazes out upon the universe unfolding before him: (See Tennyson's "Lucretius.")

The divine power and quiet dwelling-place of the gods becomes visible:
Which no winds shake, nor clouds sprinkle with showers,
Nor does white snow, hardened by sharp frost, falling violate,
And a sky forever cloudless covers it,
And broadly smiles with diffused light.

44. The word "μάλ'" qualifies "ἀνέφελος" (cloudless). Adverbs, even in prose, may be separated from the words they modify; those of place, time, and manner frequently, those of degree at times. Short, Essay, p. lxv. — "αἴθρη" is a feminine form of "αἰθήρ" (clear sky).

45. "πέπταται" means "is outspread," as a garment, ζ 94. The clouds are all below the divine abode, and form the rampart that shuts heaven from earth. ἁλιπόρφυρα [sea-purple]; references at ζ 306, ν 108, 85, θ 84, 373, η 337. Doubtless the Phoenician purple from the sea-shell murex is intended, for this was introduced at a very early period into Greece. Yet Mr. Gladstone has shown that the color-sense in the Homeric poems, as in the Vedas, is narrow, weak, indistinct, and confused, though the perceptions of light not decomposed, as varying between light and dark, white and black, are most vivid and effective; accordingly, the descriptions of color generally tend a good deal to range themselves in a scale of degrees, rather than kinds, of light. The chief king, Agamemnon, summons the βουλή in the Iliad. During all the twenty years' absence of Odysseus from Ithaca, no βουλή had been convened. But the Iliad shows us government in the unsettled condition of war, and the council is called together under extraordinary circumstances. In Scheria is depicted a normal state of peace, where the βουλή appears to be a regular senate convened at stated periods, at which it was the duty of the king to be present, a fact intimated by the imperfect tense; cf. o 468. — Φαίηκες ἀγανοί [the gentle Phaeacians], probably meaning the kings; cf. ν 120, 12, θ 428, 389–93.

What is the prose form? — θαλερὸν . . ., "youth's spring-time marriage openly to name." θαλερός, from θάλλω, "to bloom," indicates that marriage took place in the flower of youth. It was regarded as necessarily accompanying arrival at suitable age. Even the gods assist in bringing it about, as for Neoptolemus and Hermione, δ 7; cf. ζ 180–81. An elderly bachelor or spinster among the freeborn is unheard of in the poems. The sanctity of the marriage tie is held inviolate among the Greeks; polygamy is unknown, and divorce unthought of. Helen resumes her original position in the halls of Menelaus upon her return, as if nothing had happened to disturb the harmony of the household. The Homeric life stands nowhere more vividly and emphatically in contrast with that of the boasted age of Athenian civilization than in the position and estimation of woman. The respect, tenderness, and honor with which she is treated are scarcely less than in our own day, and nowhere in the poems is this more beautifully depicted than in this Phaeacian episode.

The yoke, often a simple cross-bar, was first tied fast to the end of the pole, then the animals were brought to their places under the yoke (Iliad 5.731), to the ends of which broad straps of leather were already attached; these collar-straps were next put round under the neck of the animal and fastened. The personal and active participation of the queen and her daughter in these homely labors is a charming sketch of simplicity of manners in the midst of great splendor of position and surroundings. Nor does this belong to the Phaeacian isle alone; it is a truthful depiction of Greek life in the Heroic Age. All the noble women in the poems are skilled at the distaff and the loom, Helen and Penelope notably so. The king is pre-eminent not only in all manly and graceful sports, in the use of arms and in the dangers of the chase, but he also gains knowledge of medicine, and Achilles is skillful with the lyre. Odysseus builds with his own hands a remarkable bedroom and bed in his palace, constructs the vessel with which he sails from Ogygia, and claims that he can reap more grain and run a better furrow down a four-acre field than the best suitor of the band, old as he appears. Indeed, respect for labor, and participation in it as a matter of course, find no exception even among the gods. Zeus and Hera harness, drive, and tend their own horses; Poseidon does the same, or takes and cares for those of Zeus. Athena and the Graces spin and weave ambrosial garments; while Hephaestus hammers and pounds, perspires and grows as begrimed as any blacksmith on earth. See ζ 305–6, η 5, θ 8, 424–38, ν 20. ἐτίθει is a form made with a connecting vowel, but actually more common than the regular ἐτίθη; H. 401 h. The imperfect tense depicts finely the mother's careful preparation and packing of the lunch for the darling of her house, and the supply is so abundant that it suffices in the sequel to satisfy also the ravenous appetite of Odysseus, who had been without food for three days, ζ 250. Another fine picture of a mother's fond anxiety for the little comforts of a child leaving home is that of Thetis in the Iliad, who had stored for Achilles to take with him a coffer full

On the table of Nestor in the camp stands a patera containing an onion, poto opson, Iliad XI 630. When Peisistratus and Telemachus are setting out from Pylos for Sparta, the housekeeper prepares for their lunch bread and wine and relishes, such as god-nurtured kings eat, Odyssey III 480. Bread is the "marrow of men," the mainstay and principal article of food: all else is a relish to the bread. Homer never mentions any other food on the table by name except bread and meat; but that vegetables were in use is quite certain; Odyssey VII 127. pantoine doubtless includes fruit from the orchard and vineyard, Odyssey VII 115–22, if not vegetables from the garden, Odyssey VII 127. — en before d' oinon goes with echeuen by tmesis; Odyssey XX 260, III 40. It was even given to young children, as when Phoenix holds it to the lips of the little Achilles, who spirts it out over his vesture in his childish waywardness, Iliad IX 491; Odyssey XVI 444. A temperate use of the beverage, however, is a characteristic of the age, and its mixture with water served to maintain this. At Rome in early days it was unlawful for women, and even for young men below the age of thirty, to drink wine except at sacrifices. In Egypt the monuments sometimes exhibit the women as indulging in it to excess.

84. ἅμα. Sentences or notions that are logically one thought should also be represented as such by joining them together by means of conjunctions. When this is not done, an abruptness is created which produces certain rhetorical effects, such as animation, crowding of thought in description, and surprise. Such asyndeton is very common in clauses which define or explain what was indistinctly or generally stated before, and where γάρ or ἄρα would naturally have stood, as γάρ does here. The omission imparts weight and emphasis to the explanatory thought. — καὶ . . . ἄλλαι, "also her attendants went besides." This apparently pleonastic use of ἄλλος is of common occurrence not only in Homer, but in prose Greek, and a similar idiom appears in Latin, German, and French. It springs from a striving after brevity of expression, and may often be translated by adverbs: "also," "besides," "as well."

The mechanism of which the poet here chiefly avails himself is, to exhibit the person under the influence of excited feelings as communing with his own mind, so that the breast of the man seems laid open before us, and, in the literal sense of the term, we read his thoughts as they flit through his bosom. Homer, however, stopped short of much that is found later — the Hamadryad and the constant nymph-companion of later days, the Satyr. The opposite point of view has been thus presented by Hayman: "The point of this simile seems to be that the hero moves forth from his covert with forlorn desperation, heedless whom or what he may encounter, even as the hungry lion endures wind and rain, and alike to him comes all prey, wild or tame. The simile dignifies a passage which seems to us perhaps to need such relief, but nothing in the whole context is more remarkable than the simple and unruffled gravity of its tone. No later poet could have attempted such a scene save in the Satyric vein." A nice critical discrepancy for the student to weigh and resolve. In considering this, as all Homeric similes, the following principles should be kept in view: No simile can, strictly speaking, be exact. The very nature of comparison implies a difference. But the intellectual age is more likely to work up fully the exact features than the imaginative. To the latter Homer belongs, and often when his similes are descriptive of the mode rather than the degree, we find that he has seized some general feature of resemblance, and has then extended or enlarged the ornamental element of the comparison beyond the limits of the comparison itself. By this means a fair field is gained by the poet for the play of his imagination, and a liveliness and separate picturesqueness are imparted to the description, which are always pleasurable; cf. Odyssey VI 232–35, VIII 521–30. — alkì, a metaplastic form; H. 199. This attribution has nothing to do with the comparison: it is descriptive of the lion, simply.

The attendants followed the first impulse and fled; the princess, by the aid of Athene and her own frank and fearless heart, overcame that impulse, and awaited the stranger. A speech more admirably contrived to effect its purpose can scarcely be pointed out even in Homer, whose speeches everywhere are wonderful specimens of argument and eloquence. Beginning with the assumption that she is a goddess, he likens her to Artemis, but if she be a mortal, her beauty must be the joy of all her dear ones; for anything comparable with it he never saw save once, a springing palm in Delos. Reverence for her beauty is so mingled with his admiration that it sustains and elevates a flattery which would be too open and unblushing in itself. A skillful hint at his former importance in the world is followed up by an appeal to her sympathies for the forlorn and shipwrecked wanderer whom the very gods are persecuting. He then reminds her of the common obligations of hospitality, in that she is the first whom he has met in the new land, and prefers a request whose very moderation is proof of the true delicacy that accompanies real want. "Of others" may be translated as if it meant "of all." This inclusion of the object being compared among the objects of comparison is similar to that of including a person or thing among those from whom they are to be distinguished (on 84), and the present time in the past, Odyssey VI.220. Compare Milton's imitation in Paradise Lost, IV.323:

"Adam the goodliest man of men since born
His sons; the fairest of her daughters Eve."

159. "prevailing by his gifts of wooing": "by his gifts prevailing." Aristotle says that the Greeks in early days were accustomed to purchase their wives from each other. The Homeric poems exhibit a transition period in this respect, as in so many others. To make large presents to the father of the bride was still the prevailing custom, and the word for "bride-gifts" for the most part represents these, as here; for the leading thought of the passage is to heighten the estimation in which the maiden is held, and this is best effected by depicting her as the object of ardent competition among numerous suitors who will pay heavily for the boon of her hand. See on 28, 287. "he might lead her home"; on 28. — A poet in the Anthology rises to a still higher flight in his panegyric:

"Happy is he who looks upon you; thrice blessed is he who hears you;
a demigod is he who loves you; and immortal is he who marries you."

161. "man." Homer's truly Greek love of the beautiful in human form has not confined that characteristic to the female sex. All of his heroes possess beauty in a marked degree. Thersites, the most contemptible wretch beneath the walls of Troy, was at the same time the most ugly. Achilles, on the other hand, the greatest of his heroes, possesses an almost superhuman beauty. The poet expressly declares, Odyssey VIII.168, that beauty is one of the three great gifts of god to man; and his reverence for it throughout the poems rises almost to a worship. It entitles Ganymede and Tithonus to immortality. The reverence, therefore, which Odysseus here professes before the maiden, who is plainly the poet's ideal of virgin beauty, must not be attributed merely to his flattering and gain-seeking tongue, but to a genuine admiration, which the plain-spoken hero neither needs nor desires to repress.

BOOK VI. 91

162. Δήλῳ (at Delos); on line 8. No other mention of Delos is found in Homer. Voss has inferred from this passage that Delos in Agamemnon's time possessed the foremost oracle of Apollo for seafarers, as Delphi did for landsmen. This conjecture gives a plausible motive for Odysseus' stopping there on his way to Troy, just as Aeneas does on his voyage to Italy. Doubtless it became a welcome haven at a very early period, for its harbor is one of the best in the Aegean. A scholiast thinks that the palm here is the same one of which much is made in the Homeridean Hymn to Apollo in connection with the birth of that god; but he overlooked the epithet νέον (young/new). In Homer no spot bears any trace of being honored as the birthplace of a god. The Apollo of our poet, in particular, is a deity too lofty and dread to have his birthplace fixed. Indeed, his birth at Delos was an Ionian and Athenian legend, never recognized by the Delphians, Boeotians, or Peloponnesians, except the Messenians. As late, however, as the time of Cicero and Pliny, a palm-tree was shown on the island which was declared to be the one under which Apollo and Artemis were born, and the same one which Odysseus saw; and a palm is found as an emblem of Delos on Greek vases.

163. The use of θάλος (branch) above seems to have suggested the comparison by ἔρνος (shoot) here. θάλος is properly a branch of the tree, ἔρνος a scion which springs from the root. Homer does not use ἔρνος like θάλος of a person, as the later poets do, but he says of Achilles "he shot up like a young plant" (ἀνέδραμεν ἔρνεϊ ἴσος), Iliad XVIII.56. The slender grace of Nausicaa, marked by the comparison with Artemis, is here again emphasized by the young palm shooting up with the straightness of the arrow. — ἐνόησα (I perceived) is also construed in this sense with "eyes" (ὀφθαλμοῖς, ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν).

165. τὴν ὁδόν, "on that journey;" cognate accusative; H. 547; cf. Odyssey VI.261, VIII.107. — ᾗ, "by which." — ἔμελλεν, 135. What other tenses of the infinitive may follow? H. 711; C. 501; G. 118, 6.

166. ὥς δ' αὔτως, "and in the self-same way." This phrase always assumes this form and place in the Homeric verse. Later it becomes ὡσαύτως. As an adverb it corresponds exactly to ὁ αὐτός (the same), αὔτως being the adverb of αὐτός. Buttmann therefore conjectured that the accent should be αὐτῶς, and this is the spelling adopted by Bekker. — ἐτεθήπεα, a pluperfect with the sense of an imperfect.

92 NOTES.

The termination is archaic, with the personal ending ν dropped, as is regularly the case in the 1st aorist; H. 351 D.

167. ἐκ, with γαίης: this is a rather unusual separation of a preposition from its noun, but see θ 149, ι 535, λ 115, and some remarkable prose examples in Prof. Short's Essay, p. lxxxiii. — δόρυ, used in the unusual sense of a standing tree. It is commonly used of the tree once cut and fashioned.

168. ὥς, "as," correlative to ὥς δ' αὔτως, not to τοῖον. The usual order of the correlatives is reversed; cf. γ 218–19, τ 224. — γύναι. From line 153 the assumption of divinity has been abandoned. Given the vividness of the Homeric conception of the scene, it seems scarcely too much to suppose that the poet imagined some gesture of dissent on the part of the maiden to have settled the question. She makes no disclaimer in her speech, as Aphrodite does in answer to Anchises in the Hymn, and as she does to Aeneas in the Aeneid, under similar circumstances. Homer turns his epic into drama more fully and frequently than any other poet. As in an unacted play, we are left to imagine the action, tone, and gesture not only of the speaker, as at ζ 206, 276, η 30, 48, λ 353, but also of the person addressed; see on η 315, and compare ε 205, κ 330, Milton, Paradise Lost, II. 689–95, Anthon on the Aeneid, III. 340. Virgil is usually much more descriptive. Compare Aen. I. 561 with the words of Nausicaa below. — δείδια; H. 319 D.; stem δFι, δέδFια = δείδια; on 121. Under the spell of her beauty he elevates his fear — his reason for assuming the position of a suppliant — onto higher ground than before, at line 147: ἄγαμαί τε τέθηπά τε, "I both revere thee and marvel." Construe σέ with the former verb, not the latter, which is intransitive.

169. δέ, "although," 108. The arrangement of sentences co-ordinately — that is, by employing co-ordinate conjunctions (H. 853, 855–67) to connect them — is doubtless the second stage of development in a language, the arrangement of clauses side by side without conjunctions being the earliest. The Greek language in the Homeric poems had reached the third stage, that of subordination (H. 853 b), but it still reverted with a lingering fondness to the earlier mode, and frequently used it where the logical connection requires a rendering in keeping with the later, full subordination; on 6, 234, θ 389, η 262.

170. χθιζός. The poets are fond of using adjectives for adverbs

BOOK VI. 93

of place, still more frequently for those of time, sometimes those of mode or manner and cause; H. 488 c.; on Book XIII line 75. — "wine-dark" (οἴνοπα) is used by Homer only of the sea and of oxen; XIII 32. "Wine-hued" is its proper sense, and wine is either red (ἐρυθρός), dark (μέλας), or gleaming (αἴθοψ), of which αἴθοψ is flashing, μέλας dark, and ἐρυθρός dark red. See on 53.

171. "And so long continually did the wave keep bearing me on, the sweeping tempests also." — The verb "was bearing" (ἐφόρει) is made to agree with the nearest noun, though referring to "squalls" (θύελλαι) as well. This is often the case even when several subjects stand before the verb, and is regular, as with us when only one precedes. As here, Book IV 628, Book XI 626, XIII 192, Book XXI 186; cf. Book VIII 277. For the thought, compare the words of Aeneas to his mother, Aeneid I. 375:

"We, swept from Troy across diverse seas, have been driven by fortune's own tempest to Libyan shores."

172. The preposition "from" (ἀπ'). Anastrophe does not take place when the preposition suffers elision, nor when "but/and" (δέ) is inserted between the preposition and its case; Book VI 107, 197, Book VIII 85. — "Ogygia's" (Ὠγυγίης) occurs in Homer only with "island" (νῆσος), and takes the same case. It is Calypso's isle, the "navel of the sea" (ὀμφαλὸς θαλάσσης), or centre of the great northern sea; on Book VIII 244. — "but now" (νῦν δ'), "now, however," pointing out the occurrence as beyond expectation; it may also refer to something unwished for, or not resulting in accordance with the circumstances. A succeeding aorist has the force of a perfect. — "has cast down" (κάββαλε), "has flung me down;" H. 73 D. — "divine power" (δαίμων). The idea of divine Providence governing the world and shaping the current of events is generally centred by Homer in Zeus, the father of gods and men, who holds the scales of fate, and on whose floor the two caskets stand which contain the varying incidents of human destiny; on line 188. Often this idea is conveyed by "god" (θεός), "the gods" (θεοί), "the immortals" (ἀθάνατοι), "divine power" (δαίμων), representing either Zeus himself or the gods in their combined action, since the polity of Olympus is founded upon that of the Greek state, and the united action of the ruler, counsellors, and people is the only proper mode of decree; on Book VIII 197.

173. "so that ... some ill" (ὄφρα . . . κακόν), "that doubtless even here I may suffer some ill." — "so that" (ὄφρα) is epic and lyric only. In final clauses the subjunctive is frequent after a leading historical tense, but here the force of "has cast down" (κάββαλε) is such that the subjunctive follows naturally; see Book IX 511, 580, Book XIII 303, Book XVI 233, Book III 15, Book XI 94, Book I 158, Book X 98.

94 NOTES.

174. παύσεσθ': supply κακὸν as subject; on θ 520. When are only diphthongs elided? H. 70 D.; ζ 307, θ 184. — ἀλλ'...: "but still many will the gods work me ere that." — πολλὰ, i.e. κακὰ from κακόν. — τελέουσι: H. 374.

175. ἄνασσ': He still retains the reverential mode of address. — σὲ...ἐς πρώτην: such a separation is strongly emphatic in itself, and still further emphasis is gained by placing σὲ at the head of the sentence, and ἐς πρώτην at the beginning of the line. Less care is taken for effect in the less pressing case ν 228. Cf. η 51–52, 89, 317–18.

177. τήνδε πόλιν, "the city here." What would the prose construction require with this phrase? H. 538; G. 141, Note 1 (c); C. 389. He has seen no city, but infers there must be one near, just as he conjectures that the habitations of men must be near because he hears the cry of nymphs.

178. ἄστυ and πόλιν are scarcely distinguished here, but the former, allied to the Sanskrit root vas, "to dwell," is properly the town considered as a dwelling-place; the latter, connected with πολύς, is the city viewed with reference to its inhabitants, hence the State. — ῥάκος, in Aeolic βράκος, showing Ϝράκος, as needed here by the metre.

179. "If haply some wrap of the vestments thou hadst when hither coming." — σπείρων, the garments for the wash; see on 69. — ἔχες: Why the indicative? H. 745; G. 221; C. 536; G. M. 49; ζ 150, 153, 282, 312, η 199, 320, 321, θ 146, 408.

180. δοίεν: H. 721, 1; G. M. 82. How is this optative distinguished from the potential? H. 722; on ζ 57; cf. 181, 244, 245, η 148, 149, 224, 314, 316, 331, 333. — φρεσὶ, 106, 118, 166, 313.

181–83. "Both a husband and a home, and a noble oneness of heart may they make to follow them; for surely nothing than this is more masterful or happy, than when a husband and wife, one-hearted in their purposes, sway a household." — κρεῖσσον, strong against δυσμενέεσσιν; ἄρειον, happy among εὐμενέτησι. With οὐ, ἄλλο may be supplied, as ν 392; cf. I 401, Soph. O. T. 428. — τοῦγε...ἢ ὅθ': the genitive after the comparative is more clearly defined by the clause introduced by ἢ ὅθ', which is only an enlargement of the demonstrative. This idiom is general from Homer down, in prose as well as poetry, and finds its counterpart in Latin, as

For two jars stand on the floor of Zeus's hall, filled with the gifts he gives — one of evils, one of blessings. To the man to whom Zeus who delights in thunder gives a mixed lot, he meets with evil at one time, good at another; but to the man to whom he gives only from the jar of griefs, he makes him an object of contempt, and bitter hunger drives him over the bright earth, and he wanders honored neither by gods nor men. Iliad XXIV, 525-33.

"Such is the thread the gods for mortals spin,
To live in woe, while they from cares are free.
Two coffers lie beside the door of Jove,
With gifts for man: one good, the other ill;
To whom from each the Lord of lightning gives,
Him sometimes evil, sometimes good befalls;
To whom the ill alone, him foul disgrace
And grinding misery o'er the earth pursue:
By god and man alike despised he roams." Derby.

Achilles applies this principle to his father Peleus, whose extraordinary fortune was to be marred by the early death of his son.

187. epei. No proper apodosis for this clause appears. The thought is broken at the end of the line, and when resumed at 191, it is resumed with a change, and epei repeated. See on z 275. — kako has been rightly understood by Eustathius as referring to degree, not moral character; cf. Xi 126, a 411, d 64, th 553.

189. ethelesen; on 37, 183. — hekasto, appositive, as alle, 138.

190. soi: when do the enclitic pronouns retain their accent? Hadley 232. What does Homer use for the enclitic soi? — tag', i.e. kaka. — tetlamen. Homer regularly uses the short -men after a short syllable, the long -nai after a long one, in the infinitive.

191. nun d', 172. "I could wish that Zeus had been more kind to thee, but though he afflict thee, yet will we not."

192. oun, correlative to epei. — deusesai must not be confused with deuterai, 44.

193. "(Of those things) which it is meet a suppliant trial-tried on meeting one (should not lack)." — on; on 150. The case is governed by me deuesthai, to be supplied in the thought. Why me rather than ou? Hadley 837; Goodwin 260, 1, Note 1.

194. ounoma; cf. eta 54, zeta 42, 102, eta 83.

197. "And upon him depend the Phaeacians' strength and

BOOK VI. 97

power." — ek governs tou. Why not ek? on 172. — echetai, middle, "hold themselves," the king being conceived as the stay to which all the people cling for safety and strength; lambda 346, theta 67.

198. He rha, "she spoke accordingly;" theta 186, 416, 469; more fully, theta 46, 482. — keleusen, "called to."

199. stete moi, "stop, I pray you." The ethical moi in this sense, especially with imperative thoughts; eta 208, 303, nu 59. — pose. She implies that the mere fact of seeing a man is no good reason for their flight. Only in the event of his being hostile would their flight be excusable; on 140, eta 10.

200. e me pou . . . phastho, "you do not say to yourselves, I hope, do you?" — e me would be ara me or mon in the Attic. What answer is implied in such questions? H. 829. — phastho; the operation of the mind in thought again represented dramatically, as in the actual self-dialogue of Odysseus above, 119, 141; on 185.

201. "For that man exists not as a living mortal, nor can he even be born," a strong asseveration of the supposition contained in the previous question, that they cannot imagine him to be a foeman. The asyndeton is causal. — houtos aner is quite indefinite. houtos is generally found before a relative sentence, seldom hode; if the latter, it is emphatic. — genetai, epic subjunctive; H. 720 e; G. M. 87; on zeta 126. Its taking ou, not me, shows its close connection with the future; compare pi 437, where Eurymachus, replying to Penelope, who has upbraided the suitors for their plots to slay her son, bids her be of good cheer:

"There is no such man, nor will there be, nor will he come to be,
who would lay hands on Telemachus, your son."

— dieros: Nausicaa has something of her father's fervor; on lambda 349, eta 167; psi 187.

202. For the rhyme, see on 61.

203. She assigns two reasons for their immunity from enemies: the special love and protection of the gods, and their remoteness from the rest of the world.

204. polyklustoi eni pontoi; this phrase occurs again only at delta 354, where it is descriptive of the island Pharos, a day's sail from Egypt, and at tau 277, of the spot in the midst of the sea, at a distance from Thrinakia, where Odysseus' bark founders, and he loses all

5

his companions. This seems to bear towards fixing the position of Scheria as insular; on 8, η 239.

205. eschатоi, "the remotest of men." The Ethiopians are likewise called "the remotest of men" at α 23, and they are situated along the stream of Oceanus to the south. The Phaeacians appear to represent loosely great distance in the opposite direction, though all indications place them far from the northern Oceanus.

206. "But some unfortunate yonder in his wanderings hither has come." The man we see yonder is no exception, for he is some unfortunate, who is here simply because he has been driven out of his course, and has reached here by chance. — The word "this here" is frequent, especially in the poets, in the adverbial use of "here," before us; "yonder," at no great distance, accompanied by a gesture indicating the position; on 170; H. 678. — The word for "wretched" is used substantively, as at κ 281, λ 80, 93. — "Wandering" occurs at η 239, θ 28, 14, ζ 278.

207. "The," as relative. The true relation of "pros" here is generally misconceived. As akin to "pro," this preposition has, with the genitive especially, the sense of "in front of," "in the sight of." Donaldson says rightly that "pros theon" means "in the eyes of the gods," "as seen by the gods." Compare our "'fore Heaven." This is further seen from the following passages: Zeus accompanies strangers at η 165; he protects because he accompanies — "Zeus is the guardian of suppliants and strangers, the god of strangers, who attends upon strangers along with those deserving of respect," at ι 270; he takes vengeance upon the one who ill-treats the suppliant, because he has a personal oversight of such an evil-doer — "Zeus of suppliants would punish them, he who watches over all other men and exacts punishment from whoever goes wrong," at ν 213; and he is a witness for suppliants — "suppliants, for whom Zeus is witness," at π 422. Hence the meaning "under the protection" usually assigned here arises from the earlier sense "under the eye of."

208. "Strangers and beggars." The word for "stranger" in its widest sense comprehends not only the suppliant, the one who appears with a suit for shelter and aid under the pressure of some calamity, and the guest proper who needs food and shelter simply because of his absence from home and the lack of inns for accommodation, but also the public beggar, the "beggar of all the people," of whom Irus in the Eighteenth Odyssey is the type. These travel about the country seeking relief in hospitality, and pay for it, in a measure, by im-

BOOK VI. 99

parting the news of which they are the gatherers and bearers. Odysseus appears at his own palace in this guise, and Antinous, the suitor, reproaches Eumaeus for inviting a beggar to the house. The swineherd answers evasively that no one would be so foolish as to invite a beggar, to eat him out of house and home, rho 387. But if the beggar came uninvited, he came as a guest-stranger (xeinos), towards whom the courtesy of the age must be extended. — "oligē..."; "small for the giver, but welcome to the recipient." Scholiast. It is a proverbial expression; xi 58, Alpha 167; Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus 5.

209. Brōsin, posin, dosis denote the result of the action. What is the usual sense of the verbal ending -sis? Hadley 460.

210. Lousate, "give him to bathe," i.e., supply him with the appliances of the bath, so that he may bathe himself. These consisted, under ordinary circumstances, of the water for the bathing-tub, and the oil for anointing, with perhaps a change of clothing. The active lousate is here used in its causative sense; Hadley 686. From what has already been said of the delicacy of the Homeric age respecting the person (note this, in the main, also in archaic art), and from the poet's handling of this whole episode, it would be hard to believe that the meaning of louō here and elsewhere could be simply "go bathe the stranger," the ablution to be performed by the maidens themselves. For this service is not merely rendered by slaves, but in the house of Nestor his youngest daughter attends Telemachus at the bath, and Helen performs a similar office for Odysseus when he enters Troy disguised as a beggar. Gladstone (Studies, II. p. 513 sq.) has shown that such a sense is not only repugnant to the entire tone of Homeric morals, but is inconsistent with the facts and the usage of the words. See eta 296 for an explanation of this use of the active given by the poet himself; and observe that, while the active occurs regularly of the part performed by the attendants, the middle is uniformly employed of the act of bathing whenever it is described; zeta 96, 227, theta 427, 449. — "hothen... anemоio," "where near by there is shelter from the wind." — epi, adverbial. — anemоio; Hadley 565. The shelter would appear from the circumstances of the description, epsilon 400-43, to have been a cliff, forming, by its projection into the sea, a harbor within which the river empties. If the river be conceived as run-

100 NOTES.

ning at an acute angle to the sea-coast on the side opposite the washing-troughs, and the bank there rising to a considerable height, the conditions will be sufficiently complied with; on 138.

211. ἀλλήλησι κέλευσαν, "called to each other." This "is a happy, picturesque touch; it shows each, uneasy under reproof, endeavoring slyly to throw the blame on her fellow, and it indicates that flight had scattered them." Hayman. See on 138, and compare O 658, where the Greeks, hemmed in about their ships by Hector's impetuous valor, after retreat stood closely massed beside their tents: for shame held them back, and fear; for they called out to one another without pause.

212. "And down then Odysseus they seated, taking him to the shelter." — κὰδ; on 100. — The pregnant construction of ἐπὶ with the accusative of motion and a verb of rest requires a verb of motion to be supplied in translation; H. 618 a; θ 469, ζ 218.

213. On 17. Such repetitions of the name and patronymic or its equivalent, so common in Homer, are intended to elevate the style and dignify the individual. The expression is more than ordinarily remarkable here, in that the subject of the formulaic phrase "as he commanded" is added, contrary to the poet's usual custom.

214. πὰρ . . . οἱ: this separation by conjunctions is one of the most common; ζ 248, 197, 230, η 70, 231, ν 27, ζ 207, 29; on 167. — The φᾶρος, like the χλαῖνα, was a large rectangular blanket-like mantle, worn loosely about the person as the outer garment, and caught over

BOOK VI. 101

the shoulder by a clasp, which was often of elaborate and curious workmanship, as that worn by Odysseus when departing for Troy, τ 226. It corresponded to the Roman toga, as the χιτών did to the tunic or under-garment. This was a sort of woollen shirt, shaped to the body, and reaching generally to the knees. It was without sleeves, or had only very short ones. See the accompanying illustration from an archaic statue of the Cesnola Collection. — εἵματα, appositive, "as garments;" a frequent formula; η 234.

216. μιν, subject accusative. — λούσθαι, "to bathe himself." The whole procedure here doubtless gives in full the usual details. After telling him that everything is ready and he can bathe in the stream, they were withdrawing to a distance, when Odysseus forestalls the movement in order to ingratiate himself with the attendants by a display of delicacy, as he had already done with their mistress by his winning courtesy and modest request.

217. δή ῥα τότ', "straightway then." This collocation of particles shows Odysseus' eagerness to anticipate their departure. When only may δή stand at the beginning of a clause? H. 851 c. — The dative of the person with μετανδάω seems to be one of place, since the simple verb regularly has an accusative, but the compound a dative, pointing to the influence of the preposition as determining the case; cf. θ 433.

218. στῆθ' . . . ἀπόπροθεν, "take your stand, going thus to a distance;" on 212. — οὕτω, "thus," as you are now doing, shows that they are already withdrawing. — ὄφρ'; on 80. When is the subjunctive used in such clauses? G. M. 66, 2; ζ 304, η 319, ζ 295, λ 351; η 141, 276, 280. — ἐγὼ αὐτὸς, "I, by myself," so that in the unembarrassed performance of the task I may be free from any hindrance from your possible proximity.

219. ὤμοιιν; 19, 82; 224. — ἀμφὶ; on 9.

220. δηρὸν gives to ἐστιν the force of a perfect; η 152, θ 36; on 158, 250.

221. ἔγωγε, "I at least," whatever a boor might do. — ἄν shifts the positive tone of the future, "I will not," to the more courteous "I would not," because it is repugnant to my feelings; G. M. 37, 2; H. 710 b. κεν is the usual particle with the future; ἄν only here and X 49, 66.

102 NOTES.

222. kourē: properly used of the freeborn, and often of the noble. It is therefore a dignifying word, and by using it here Odysseus further wins the goodwill of the attendants by implying his belief that they are above the common station of amphipoloi (servant-maids).

223. eipon, "told it," that is, his delicate courtesy and the good impression he had made upon them. This, coupled with apaneuthen, shows that the princess had purposely gone to a distance along the seashore where her attendants would join her.

224. ho ek: this hiatus is not unusual, especially after autar ho; Odyssey Book 7, line 230, Book 8, line 396. What words are exempt from elision? Hadley's Grammar, section 70. — ek potamou: The usual custom where conveniences were at hand appears to be illustrated at Book 10, line 361, where Odysseus in the palace of Circe is made to seat himself in the bathing-tub and wash from a large tripod, pouring the water down over head and shoulders. ek potamou and perhaps eisan appear to show conformance with the custom here. — nizeto, with a double accusative like verbs of depriving; see the genitive at line 219; Hadley 553; Goodwin 164; Curtius 402.

225. nota: see note on line 107. — ampexen: why not amphexen? Hadley 65d.

226. atrugeto, "vintageless," "unharvested;" see Book 7, line 124. This is the specific epithet of hals, thalassa, pontos, and of aither, in opposition to the land, which is polyphorbos, polyboteira.

227-28. panta, supply chroa (the whole body). — aleipsen, active, for metrical convenience. — amphi: see note on line 100; "and about him the garments had been thrown."

229. men begins the apodosis of epeide. — Dios: see Hadley 572d. — ekgegauia, like Virgil's "born of Ammon," "son of a goddess," etc.

230-31. "Both taller to look upon and portlier, and down from his head she showered his thick locks, the hyacinth blossom matching." — eisideein: what voice is used in this construction? Goodwin-Middleton 93, 2. How is passona formed from pachion? Hadley 60. This heightening of personal graces for a special purpose is resorted to again on the following morning, when Odysseus is to appear before the critical eyes of the whole Phaeacian people (Book 8, line 19), and on another occasion when he is to be recognized by Penelope (Book 23, line 157). Penelope herself is in like manner adorned by the goddess when she purposes to present herself before the suitors to complain of their omission to offer the customary

gifts, sigma 195; and Laertes is renewed with additional youth after his recognition of Odysseus, omega 369. All these involve no absolute change in the appearance, further than to heighten and reanimate what is already there, fill up the toil-worn or grief-worn limbs, and bring back the springing step and lofty bearing. Flowing hair was a characteristic of the Greeks of the Heroic Age, as of the Spartans later; their care of it is evidenced by the common phrase "long-haired Achaeans." The word oulас, identical in root with holos (whole), is here "thick and heavy," representing the vigorous growth of manly strength. Am. The likeness to the flower of the hyacinth has generally been found in its dark color. But Homer is not accustomed to make his similes turn upon color. They are rich in the use of motion, force, form, sound, symmetry, number; but Mr. Gladstone finds only three color similes out of some two hundred, at Delta 141, Xi 14, and Rho 547. Again, the color which fills the ideal of beauty for the hair, and forms the crowning glory of his great heroes, is blonde or auburn, as that of Menelaus, Achilles, etc. It is true that the extraordinary mental gifts of Odysseus everywhere so far overshadow his bodily qualities that the latter are seldom mentioned; yet it is clear that he lacks but one of the Homeric elements of beauty—stature. He is shorter by a head than the lofty-statured Agamemnon, but he is more stately than Menelaus. Yet at nu 399 and 431 he is distinctly stated to have fair hair; and if those passages are genuine, as is usually conceded, at least for one, the same color must be supposed here; for no change affecting that is made from this point on to the transformation of nu. The difficulty remains, however, that at pi 175, where he is retransformed, to be recognized by his son, we find the expression "he became dark-complexioned, and his beard became dark," which has appeared inconsistent with auburn hair. But it must be remembered that the poet is treating of a change from the white complexion and white beard of decrepit age, nu 430–32, pi 182, sigma 355, to the strength and color of active manhood, and the verb geneto is to be noted, "he became dark-skinned" from white, and his beard "became darkened" from white. The ruddy tan and sunburn of a man much in the open air, and the ruddy beard usual with auburn hair, would satisfy the epithets; cf. mu 243, Virgil, Aeneid VIII. 64, IX. 816. Even light hair with a black-

Egyptian paintings represent the Creteward enemies of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties as fair, with aquiline nose, blue eyes, short red beard, and hair formally curled. 232. "gold ... silver" — the verb περιχεύεται (poured around), aorist subjunctive, is most commonly found in Homeric similes, though the present tense also occurs. The comparison is taken from the realm of the metal-worker's art. Just as the craftsman imparts additional splendor to already beautiful silver by plating it with gold, so the art of Athene bestows that same enhancement upon Odysseus. Plating with gold is often mentioned. Nestor gilds the horns of the sacrificial victim he is to offer to Athene; the silver wool-basket of Helen is worked around the rim with gold; see Odyssey θ 403, 430. Gold was more abundant than silver in the Homeric age, yet at the same time more valuable. Numerous objects of silver plated with gold were discovered by Schliemann at Mycenae, but invariably a thin plate of copper was found between the two metals, as if the goldsmith found it easier to plate gold onto copper than directly onto silver.

233. Hephaistos teaches the metal-worker as the god who presides over that particular branch of art; but Athene, as ruler of the wider sphere of all art and handiwork. As a female deity, she particularly imparts skill in spinning, weaving, embroidery, and other accomplishments of her sex; but she also teaches measurement to the carpenter, and presides over industry in general. — δέδαεν (she has taught); θ 481.

The change wrought in the squalid sea-waif is so great that it must needs have been done by a god; he must therefore be under the protection of the dwellers of Olympus. — "In front of," as applied to place, means "in front of"; see note on 207. We generally view the past as behind us, the future as before us. Homer, on the contrary, conceived the past as in front, the future behind, as in his description of the prophetic powers of Calchas, Iliad A 70: who knew the things that are, the things that will be, and the things that were before. After the present and the future, "that which is in front" must be the past. A vestige of the same view appears in our word "before," which may be employed to translate the Greek word here.

He has already hinted his former importance in the world, and it is not unusual in the poems to find outer comeliness taken to argue mental and moral qualities of worth, which in this case have been proved as well by his speech as by his bearing throughout. All this conspires to present the thought to her in the light of a possibility, and the frankness of her nature reveals it to her companions, but the poet has been careful that it shall not reach the ears of Odysseus.

"Ravenously; for long without taste of food had he been." — ἁρπαλέως; on 30. — Just as δηρόν above, 220, gave to the present the force of a perfect, so here it makes the imperfect equivalent to a pluperfect. — ἐδητύος; H. 584 b. 251–52. On 111, 112.

When the partitive genitive is dependent upon a relative pronoun, the commonest position for it is immediately before the relative, as theta 204; but sometimes separated from it, as here. If placed after the relative, it is regularly separated from it, as eta 156, 322.

263. hekaterthe (on each side), 19. — poles, 40. The situation is that of a city built upon a peninsula, something like that of New York, with a harbor on each side, and a narrow neck of land connecting the peninsula with the mainland. This neck is the eisithme or entrance to the city from the country. The end of the peninsula towards the sea appears to have been unfitted for landing, by reason of its elevation and ruggedness along shore, or lack of shelter. The dock-yards were consequently built along the low neck of land, and occupied both sides of the single road-way leading into the city, so that the ships, drawn up upon their rests out of the water, as was customary in the Homeric day, seemed to form a rampart along the road-side, and guard the way.

The word eiruatai; H. 405 D. b. — pasin ... hekasto, "for all (the Phaeacians) have a boat-house each." — pasin; H. 598. — hekasto, 189. — Ammonius, deriving epistion from epi stenai, explains it as a place for the ship to stand upon when drawn out of the water; but the view of the scholiasts, that besides the mere rest there was also a covering over them to shelter from sun and rain, seems more reasonable, as they were for permanent use; on n 77. 266. Phaeacian devotion to the sea is marked not only by the fact that every man has a pinnace of his own, but by their establishing their agora hard by the ships, though at Troy it was beside Priam's palace, and in the camp of the Greeks near its centre. The agora then, as later, was the common resort of the men, whether any public business was being done or not. No regular assembly of the people had taken place in Ithaca since the departure of Odysseus, till convoked by Telemachus, b 7, and no other is spoken of from that time till after the death of the suitors; yet Telemachus goes to the agora on the morning following his return from Sparta, evidently expecting to find, and does find, the people gathered there. He does the same on the succeeding morning, as if it were a matter of course. See o 468, k 114. — "around a beautiful shrine of Poseidon." — The word Posideion appears nowhere else in Homer as a substantive, but at B 506 as an adjective, Posideion aglaon alsos. This has probably led one of the scholiasts to interpret it here as a grove or glebe, and Mr. Gladstone urges this view. That, however, accords rather with the unsettled condition of a camp, as before Troy, or a primitive country life, than a wealthy and peaceful city. Furthermore, the poet has expressly stated that Nausithous founded temples when the city was built,

and we have no other mention of them unless this is one. Gladstone himself says that in the agora "the public solemnities of religion were performed, and there were gathered into a focus the religious as well as the patriotic sentiments of the country." Hence we should naturally look there for a temple, and that too of their tutelary divinity. We can have little doubt who that greatest of the gods would be to a people so pre-eminently devoted to the sea, and the sequel shows that Poseidon regards them as his actual offspring, and it is he that endows them with their miraculous speed upon his element; Book XIII line 130, Book VIII line 35. Virgil unites both grove and temple, Aeneid I. 441. — The word ἀμφὶς stands mostly after its case, but, like ἀμφὶ, it does not shift its accent.

267. "With hauled stones in the earth fast set." Three explanations have been given for this; the first of which, namely, that of a stone pavement, may be rejected at once, not because that would be an anachronism, as Merry says, for Schliemann discovered a paved street at Troy, twenty-five feet below the surface; but because the athletic exercises of Book VIII, performed in the agora, would not have been held on a paved surface. Of the other two, the weight of authority leans towards a wall of Cyclopean architecture enclosing the square. In the only passage where κατωρυχέεσσι occurs elsewhere, it is employed of the stones forming the wall of the court-yard before the cave of Polyphemus. In like manner ῥυτοῖσιν is found only once more, at Book XIV line 10, and there of the stones used by Eumaeus in constructing the enclosure of his court-yard. Others, however, refer the stones to the seats mentioned at Book VIII line 6; cf. Book II line 99, Book XVIII line 504, Book II line 14. Schliemann's excavations in the acropolis of Mycenae unearthed a circular enclosure about one hundred feet in diameter, formed of two rows of slabs set upright in the earth, and dove-tailed together at the top by a third slab covering them. The upright slabs leaned somewhat towards the centre, thus forming both enclosure and seats, and combining the diverse views here, if Schliemann's interpretation of it be accepted. The Phaeacian agora is of great size compared with that. Of porticos and other decorative structures which adorned the agoras of the later Greeks, Homer makes no mention.

An engaging forwardness is thus rescued from the verge of boldness by an expedient which Pope declares to be "an instance of the great art of Homer in saying everything properly." 277. "And where was she so fortunate as to find him? A husband now will she have of her own choice." It is wrong to translate the Greek word as "picked up," as some have done; the verb eurisko means to find what one seeks, and, as Eustathius has said, is here used of a piece of good-fortune. The noun eurhema means a lucky find. By the dramatic method, Nausicaa is returning some of the compliments which Odysseus had paid her in his first speech. She was beautiful as Artemis, possibly a nymph; he is handsome and majestic, nay, perhaps a god. The bitter sarcasm which many have seen in the entire speech is totally at variance with the feelings of the princess, and lies rather in the mind of the commentator than in the language of the poet. No slighting or unkindly words should fall from her lips. — "herself," delta 118; on 282.

280. "Or else to her beseeching some long-prayed-for god has come." Nitzsch, while disposed to retain the remainder of the

passage, would reject this and the following line. They are, however, exactly to the point. Despairing of a release from the indignity of a union with native suitors, the maiden's prayer turns even to the gods. Nor need such a prayer be deemed presumptuous on her part. Poseidon himself is her great-grandfather, and the gods are wont to come familiarly to fraternize and feast with the Phaeacians, who are of their kin; Odyssey Book 7, lines 56–66, 199–206. The poet who represents the sea-nymph Thetis as married to Peleus and living for many years in his palace would surely feel no difficulty in the idea of such a union among the semi-divine Phaeacians. In fact we have a similar prayer from the mouth of the Greek Antiope, Book 11, line 261.

281. "and will have her to wife."

282. "All the better is it if she even herself personally going to him has found a husband from abroad" (than that she should remain unwedded as she bids fair to do). The word "better" commonly occurs where two disagreeable alternatives present themselves and the lesser of two evils is chosen. Here the two are, on the one hand, no marriage at all, and on the other, an indelicate forwardness that transgresses the widest limits of decorum. But the latter, bad as it is, is preferable to the unheard-of refusal to marry altogether; see note on line 66. Situated as we are, she ought to abandon all her old notions of caste and wed a Phaeacian; but if she persists in her pride of station, it is better that she find her equal from abroad. The form "herself" stands for "and herself." Both "and" and "even" emphasize "herself." Lines 278–84 appear to be answers to the thoughts contained in 276–77. There are two questions and one assertion. "Who is the stranger?" finds its answer in "some foreigner, or else a god." "Where did she find him?" — "She brought him from some ship, or else he comes from heaven." "Now she will have a husband" is addressed by "better that she should than to go unwedded, even though she has been so unmaidenly as to seek out a husband and make the choice herself." The chief censure lies in "herself" at line 277, and "herself even going to him," as proved by lines 286–88, where the thought is recapitulated.

M. 32; 63, 4 (b.).
